facts.value: During the 14th–17th centuries, the Bhakti movement swept through Central and Northern India. It started in the eighth century in south India (Tamil Nadu and Kerala) and spread northwards.
Dnyaneshwar, Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, Vallabhacharya, Surdas, Meera Bai, Kabir, Tulsidas, Ravidas, Namdeo, Eknath, Ramdas, Tukaram, and other mystics were some of the saints in the North.
They taught that people could cast aside the burdens of ritual and caste and simply express their overwhelming love for God.
Many Hindu groups regarded as outside the traditional Hindu caste system followed Bhakti traditions by worshipping saints belonging to their communities.
The Kabir Panth is a religious movement based on the teachings of the Indian poet saint Kabir (1398–1518).
Kabir sermonised a monotheism that appealed to the poor and convinced them of their access to God with no liaison.
Kabir denied both Hinduism and Islam and condemned double standards.
Guru Nanak Dev Ji (1469–1539) was the founder of Sikhism.
Sikhism recognizes all humans as equal before Waheguru, regardless of colour, caste, or lineage.
Christianity was believed to be introduced to India by Thomas the Apostle in 52 CE.
Jews first arrived as traders from Judea in the city of Kochi, Kerala, in 562 BCE.
Islam came to India in the early 7th century through the Arab traders in Malabar coast.
Islam is the second largest religion in India, with 14.2% of the country's population identifying as adherents.
